claim: Serial block-face scanning electron microscopy (SBF-SEM) was used to reconstruct the internal 3D structures of Nilaparvata lugens at nanometer resolution for the first time.
source: Using serial block-face scanning electron microscopy, we report on the internal 3D structures of the brown planthopper, Nilaparvata lugens (Hemiptera: Delphacidae) at nanometer resolution for the first time.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the method used and the achievement of nanometer resolution for the first time.

claim: Three four-way rings connect adjacent spiracles in Nilaparvata lugens to facilitate efficient gas exchange.
source: Within the reconstructed organs and tissues, we found many novel and fascinating internal structures in the planthopper such as naturally occurring three four-way rings connecting adjacent spiracles to facilitate efficient gas exchange
evidence: The abstract describes the discovery of three four-way rings connecting spiracles, supported by the 3D reconstruction data.

claim: Fungal endosymbionts in Nilaparvata lugens occupy a single huge insect cell that takes up 22% of the abdomen volume.
source: fungal endosymbionts in a single huge insect cell occupying 22% of the abdomen volume to enable the insect to live on plant sap
evidence: The abstract states the percentage of abdominal volume occupied by the mycetocyte containing fungal endosymbionts, which is quantified from reconstruction data.

claim: The protractors of the stylets contract during feeding in Nilaparvata lugens, which is unexpected.
source: The results revealed an unexpected contraction of the protractors of the stylets and suggested a novel feeding model for the phloem sap-sucking.
evidence: The abstract explicitly describes the unexpected finding of protractor contraction during feeding.

claim: A novel feeding model for phloem sap-sucking is proposed based on the muscle and stylet movement observations.
source: The results revealed an unexpected contraction of the protractors of the stylets and suggested a novel feeding model for the phloem sap-sucking.
evidence: The abstract states that a novel feeding model is suggested based on the reconstruction results.

claim: SBF-SEM allows visualization of insect internal structure at nanometer resolution in 3D.
source: Serial block-face scanning electron microscopy (SBF-SEM) allows visualization of the insect's internal structure at the nanometer resolution in 3D.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the capability of SBF-SEM for nanometer resolution 3D visualization.

claim: SBF-SEM relies on reiterated imaging and sectioning of resin embedded samples using a robotic ultramicrotome and digital assembly of single images to 3D images.
source: This method relies on reiterated imaging and sectioning of resin embedded sample using a robotic ultramicrotome and digital assembly of the single images to 3D images (Denk and Horstmann, 2004).
evidence: The introduction describes the technical basis of SBF-SEM with a citation to the original method.

claim: The resolution of micro-CT is insufficient to distinguish details in small insects and delicate structures.
source: However, for small insects and delicate structures, the resolution of micro-CT is insufficient to distinguish details.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states the limitation of micro-CT for small insects.

claim: Reconstruction of a 3D atlas of the whole body of any insect by EM method has not been conducted yet.
source: Although reconstruction of a 3D atlas of the whole body of any insect by EM method is valuable and theoretically possible, it has not been conducted yet.
evidence: The introduction explicitly states that whole-body insect reconstruction by EM has not been done before this study.

claim: Hemipteran insects possess delicate mouthparts with straw-like stylets that are highly specialized for penetrating plant tissues.
source: Hemipteran insects are in general small and possess delicate mouthparts with straw-like stylets that are highly specialized for penetrating plant tissues.
evidence: The introduction describes the morphological characteristics of hemipteran mouthparts.

claim: Hemipterans are proposed to protrude their stylets by contracting the respective muscles, but evidence of muscle movement has not been provided.
source: When sucking in plant sap, hemipterans are proposed to protrude their straw-like stylets into the plant tissue by contracting the respective muscles (Leopold et al., 2003; Beardsley and Gonzalez, 1975), but an evidence of the muscle movement has not been provided.
evidence: The introduction states that the proposed mechanism lacks direct evidence of muscle movement.

claim: The commonly assumed feeding mechanism for phloem sap-sucking insects was largely speculative instead of being based on actual movement of muscles and feeding apparatuses.
source: Indeed, the commonly assumed feeding mechanism for phloem sap-sucking insects was largely speculative instead of being based on the actual movement of muscles and the feeding apparatuses.
evidence: The introduction explicitly characterizes previous feeding mechanism models as speculative.

claim: Nilaparvata lugens damages rice by directly feeding and ovipositing on it and by transmitting two rice viruses.
source: They damage rice not only by directly feeding and ovipositing on it but also by transmitting two rice viruses, rice rugged stunt virus and rice grassy stunt virus.
evidence: The introduction describes the multiple ways BPH damages rice plants.

claim: Dense BPH infestations can cause complete drying and wilting of rice plants, a condition known as 'hopperburn'.
source: Dense BPH infestations can cause complete drying and wilting of rice plants, a condition known as 'hopperburn'.
evidence: The introduction explicitly defines the term 'hopperburn' and its cause.

claim: BPH outbreaks have been re-occurring approximately every 3 years in Asian countries since the late 1960s.
source: Since the late 1960s, BPH outbreaks have been re-occurring approximately every 3 years in Asian countries, with their annual outbreak area amounting to approximately 10–20 million hectares of rice, resulting in millions of tons of losses.
evidence: The introduction provides historical data on BPH outbreak frequency and impact.

claim: BPHs seasonally migrate from their overwintering rice fields in tropical Asia northward to temperate areas in China, Korea, Japan, and northern India.
source: BPHs seasonally migrate from their overwintering rice fields in tropical Asia northward to temperate areas in China, Korea, Japan, and northern India when rice becomes available, inflicting damage in an even larger area across Asia (Perfect and Cook, 1994).
evidence: The introduction describes the migration pattern of BPH with a citation.

claim: The length of the insect (Nilaparvata lugens nymph) measures approximately 600 µm.
source: The length of the insect measures approximately 600 µm (Figure 1).
evidence: The results section provides a direct measurement of the insect length.

claim: 24 neuropils were found in the central nerve system of Nilaparvata lugens.
source: We discover several novel and fascinating internal structures in BPH, such as 24 neuropils in the central nerve system (Figure 1—figure supplement 1)
evidence: The results section states the number of neuropils discovered, with reference to a figure showing the reconstruction.

claim: The fungal endosymbionts in Nilaparvata lugens occupy a single huge mycetocyte that takes up 22% of the abdominal volume and 4.2% of the total body volume.
source: fungal endosymbionts in a single huge mycetocyte occupying 22% of the abdominal volume to enable the host to thrive on a low-nutrient diet provided solely by rice (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D, Table 2).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative measurements of mycetocyte volume with reference to figures and a table.

claim: The alimentary canal of Nilaparvata lugens includes the esophagus, the anterior diverticulum, the midgut, and the hindgut and ends with the anus.
source: The alimentary canal starts with specialized mouthparts and includes the esophagus, the anterior diverticulum (AD) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), the midgut (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), and the hindgut (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F) and ends with the anus (Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: The results section describes the components of the alimentary canal with references to figures.

claim: The anterior diverticulum extends anteriorly into the head of Nilaparvata lugens.
source: The anterior diverticulum (AD) extends anteriorly into the head (Figure 2A,B, Interactive 3D-PDF).
evidence: The results section describes the anatomical position of the anterior diverticulum with figure references.

claim: The midgut of Nilaparvata lugens is divided into an anterior sac and a midgut loop.
source: The midgut is divided into an anterior sac and a midgut loop (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,E).
evidence: The results section describes the division of the midgut with figure references.

claim: The inner surface of the whole midgut is covered by a dense layer of microvilli.
source: The inner surface of the whole midgut is covered by a dense layer of microvilli, especially in the loop region where the gut lumen is almost constricted (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The results section describes the microstructure of the midgut surface with a figure reference.

claim: There is no filter chamber in Nilaparvata lugens.
source: There is no membrane or sheath enveloping the midgut loop, and the filter chamber, which is a common structure in sap-sucking Hemipteran insects, is not found (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The results section explicitly states the absence of a filter chamber with a figure reference.

claim: Three structurally different endosymbionts are distributed in the Nilaparvata lugens nymph.
source: The 3D reconstruction reveals the distribution of three structurally different endosymbionts in the nymph.
evidence: The results section states the number of different endosymbiont types found.

claim: The most generally distributed endosymbiont in Nilaparvata lugens is the Ascomycete fungus Entomomyces delphacidicola, also known as yeast-like symbionts (YLSs).
source: The most generally distributed endosymbiont is the Ascomycete fungus Entomomyces delphacidicola (Fan et al., 2015), also known as the yeast-like symbionts (YLSs), which have an ellipsoidal shape from a few microns to over 10 microns (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The results section identifies the most common endosymbiont with a citation and figure references.

claim: Two fat body mycetocytes adjacent to the midgut are full of thread-like bacterial endosymbionts.
source: Another two fat body mycetocytes adjacent to the midgut (Figure 2C,F) are full of thread-like bacterial endosymbionts.
evidence: The results section describes the location and contents of two mycetocytes with figure references.

claim: 10 hollow cells in the wall of the anterior diverticulum each accommodate numerous rod-like bacterial endosymbionts.
source: in the wall we found 10 hollow cells that each accommodates numerous rod-like bacterial endosymbionts (Figure 2C,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B)
evidence: The results section provides a count of specialized cells containing endosymbionts with figure references.

claim: 95% of the symbionts in the anterior diverticulum are Arsenophonus species.
source: 16S rDNA sequence of the AD showed that 95% of the symbionts are Arsenophonus species (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative data from 16S rDNA sequencing with a figure reference.

claim: The volume of total tracheae in the first instar nymph was 24,000 µm3, accounting for about 0.1% of the body volume.
source: The volume of total tracheae in the first instar nymph was 24,000 µm3, accounting only for about 0.1% of the body volume (Table 2).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative measurements of tracheal volume with a table reference.

claim: Two pairs of thoracic spiracles and eight pairs of abdominal spiracles make up the tracheal network in Nilaparvata lugens.
source: Two pairs of thoracic spiracles (ts1 and ts2), eight pairs of abdominal spiracles (as1–as8), and tracheae extending from the spiracles make up the network (Figure 2D).
evidence: The results section describes the components of the tracheal system with a figure reference.

claim: Every abdominal spiracle in Nilaparvata lugens is embedded in a pitting called the atrium with two valves.
source: Every abdominal spiracle is embedded in a pitting called the atrium with two valves, one of which separated the trachea and the atrium, while the other one divides the atrium into two parts (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The results section describes the structure of abdominal spiracles with a figure reference.

claim: All the spiracles in Nilaparvata lugens are connected by dorsal longitudinal trunks.
source: All the spiracles are connected by dorsal longitudinal trunks (dlt) (Figure 2D).
evidence: The results section describes the tracheal connections with a figure reference.

claim: Three four-way tracheal rings at the ventral side connect adjacent spiracles and their counterparts at the other side of the body.
source: Three four-way tracheal rings at the ventral side connect the adjacent two spiracles and their counterparts at the other side of the body, like a traffic circle (Figure 2D,H–J).
evidence: The results section describes the novel tracheal ring structures with figure references.

claim: The beak of Nilaparvata lugens is formed of the labium under a conical labrum.
source: The beak is formed of the labium under a conical labrum (Figure 3E, Figure 3—figure supplement 1C, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The results section describes the external morphology of the mouthparts with figure references.

claim: The labium of Nilaparvata lugens is 130 μm in length with three segments.
source: The labium is 130 μm in length with three segments, but only the second (L2) and third segments (L3) are seen from the ventral side, as the first segment (L1) is covered by the labrum (Figure 4A, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The results section provides a measurement of labium length with figure references.

claim: The stylet bundle consists of two mandibular stylets and two maxillary stylets.
source: The stylet bundle consists of two mandibular stylets and two maxillary stylets.
evidence: The results section describes the composition of the stylet bundle.

claim: The two maxillary stylets are interlocked by longitudinal ridges and grooves.
source: The two maxillary stylets are interlocked by longitudinal ridges and grooves (Figure 3F).
evidence: The results section describes the structural features of maxillary stylets with a figure reference.

claim: The food canal and the saliva canal are formed where the two maxillary stylets meet.
source: The food canal and the saliva canal are formed where the two maxillary stylets meet.
evidence: The results section describes the formation of canals in the stylet bundle.

claim: The principle gland of Nilaparvata lugens is acinar, with nine kinds of follicles (A–I).
source: The principle gland is acinar, with nine kinds of follicles (A–I).
evidence: The results section describes the structure and composition of the principle salivary gland.

claim: Follicles A and B in the principle gland each include six binucleate cells.
source: In follicles A and B, by contrast, the boundaries between the cells are clear. Both include six binucleate cells (A1–A6 and B1–B6) (Figure 5B).
evidence: The results section provides a count of cells in specific follicles with a figure reference.

claim: The cibarial pump is a sclerotized-walled canal with quadrangle cross sections.
source: The extreme anterior end of the esophagus, the cibarial pump, is a sclerotized-walled canal with quadrangle cross sections (Figure 3A).
evidence: The results section describes the structure of the cibarial pump with a figure reference.

claim: In feeding modality, the protractors of the stylets are shortened and retractors are all elongated.
source: In feeding modality, unexpectedly, the protractors of the stylets are shortened and retractors are all elongated (Figure 4D,D', E,E').
evidence: The results section describes the unexpected muscle states during feeding with figure references.

claim: The lb/wh ratio of feeding nymphs (0.530 ± 0.065) is significantly smaller than that of relaxed nymphs (0.801 ± 0.069).
source: The lb/wh ratio of the 19 feeding nymphs is 0.530 ± 0.065 (mean ± SEM), significantly smaller than that of the 12 relaxed nymphs with the ratio of 0.801 ± 0.069 (mean ± SEM, Figure 4C).
evidence: The results section provides quantitative measurements with statistical comparison and a figure reference.

claim: SBF-SEM is well suitable for entomological studies.
source: Although the majority of SBF-SEM data are collected in neuroscience studies and the sample preparation methods are optimized for brains and neuronal tissues (Denk and Horstmann, 2004; Tapia et al., 2012), SBF-SEM is well suitable for entomological studies.
evidence: The discussion section explicitly states the suitability of SBF-SEM for entomological studies with citations.

claim: SBF-SEM can handle large samples like insects of several hundred microns and small samples like collagen fibrils.
source: SBF-SEM can handle large samples like insects of several hundred microns and small samples like collagen fibrils (Starborg et al., 2013).
evidence: The discussion section describes the range of sample sizes SBF-SEM can handle with a citation.

claim: The waterproof exoskeleton of insects prevents normal fixation and staining.
source: Compared with brains and tissue blocks, the waterproof exoskeleton of insects prevents normal fixation and staining.
evidence: The discussion section identifies a challenge in preparing insect samples for SBF-SEM.

claim: Protrusion of the stylet in Nilaparvata lugens results mainly by lowering the head and compression of the labium.
source: In contrast, we found that the protractor muscles did not contract even when the stylet tips were pushed out of the beak, which was beyond previous conception. Protrusion of the stylet resulted mainly by lowering the head and compression of the labium.
evidence: The discussion section proposes a mechanism based on the observed muscle states.

claim: The planthopper stylet penetration mechanism might apply to most sap-sucking hemipterans with short stylets.
source: Overall, the planthopper stylet penetration mechanism might apply to most sap-sucking hemipterans with short stylets.
evidence: The discussion section generalizes the findings to other hemipteran species.

claim: The filter chamber is not present in Nilaparvata lugens.
source: However, a filter chamber is not present in N. lugens, and a different water-disposal mechanism is proposed.
evidence: The discussion section explicitly states the absence of a filter chamber.

claim: Water in the sap may be transported to the end of the midgut loop through the epithelia at the point where the distal end of the anterior midgut contacts the anterior midgut.
source: At this place, water in the sap may be transported to the end of the loop region through the epithelia, thereby concentrating proteins and lipid that may then move into the anterior part of the midgut loop for further digestion and absorption.
evidence: The discussion section proposes a mechanism for water transport based on structural observations.

claim: Members of the suborder Auchenorrhyncha have filter chambers with exception of those species belonging to Fulgoroidea.
source: Members of the suborder Auchenorrhyncha have filter chambers with exception of those species belonging to Fulgoroidea (Hickernell, 1923; Kershaw, 1914; Zhong et al., 2015).
evidence: The discussion section describes the distribution of filter chambers in Auchenorrhyncha with citations.

claim: The yeast-like fungus is an obligate endosymbiont in the planthopper.
source: The yeast-like fungus is an obligate endosymbiont in the planthopper. They cannot survive in vitro and usually reside in the fat body mycetocytes, though in this case, we found some of them in legs and heads.
evidence: The discussion section characterizes the yeast-like symbionts as obligate endosymbionts.

claim: Genes involved in the synthesis of essential amino acids and cholesterol are found in the genome of the yeast-like symbionts but not in the BPH genome.
source: Fan et al., 2015 revealed that genes involved in the synthesis of essential amino acids and cholesterol are found in the genome of the yeast-like symbionts but not in the BPH genome, indicating that the yeast-like symbionts provide essential amino acids and cholesterol to their host.
evidence: The discussion section cites genomic evidence for the nutritional role of yeast-like symbionts.

claim: Yeast-like symbionts are maternally transmitted to the eggs and are present in all developmental stages of the host insect.
source: Yeast-like symbionts are maternally transmitted to the eggs and are present in all developmental stages of the host insect (Cheng and Hou, 2001).
evidence: The discussion section describes the transmission mode of yeast-like symbionts with a citation.

claim: The mycetocyte containing yeast-like symbionts is likely to grow bigger as the symbionts thrive, but it does not undergo cell division during the embryonic and nymphal stages.
source: The mycetocyte is likely to grow bigger as the symbionts thrive, but it does not undergo a cell division during the embryonic and nymphal stages.
evidence: The discussion section proposes a growth pattern for the mycetocyte based on observations.

claim: The dominant microbe in the anterior diverticulum is Arsenophonus species.
source: Our 16 s sequencing results showed that the dominant microbe in the AD is Arsenophonus species, which is reported to kill the male eggs in the wasp, Nasonia vitripennis but in N. lugens shows effect on host insecticide resistance (Pang et al., 2018).
evidence: The discussion section reports the results of 16S sequencing with a citation.

claim: The four-way tracheal ring that connects nearby four spiracles is a structure found in insects for the first time.
source: The four-way tracheal ring that connects nearby four spiracles is a structure found in insects for the first time.
evidence: The discussion section explicitly states this is a novel finding.

claim: The volume of total tracheae in N. lugens accounted for about 0.12% of the body volume.
source: The volume of total tracheae in N. lugens accounted for about 0.12% of the body volume.
evidence: The discussion section provides a quantitative measurement of tracheal density.

claim: The tracheal density in N. lugens is relatively low compared to other insects.
source: Compared to the tracheal density of 0.5% in Tribolium castaneum (Coleoptera: Tenebrionidea), 4.8% in Eleodes obscura (Coleoptera: Tenebrionidea) calculated using the stereological point count method (Kaiser et al., 2007), and 0.6% in Tenebrio molitor (Coleoptera: Tenebrionidea) larva (Raś et al., 2018), the tracheal density in N. lugens is relatively low.
evidence: The discussion section compares tracheal density across species with citations.

claim: The planthopper has a simplified tracheal system without ventral longitudinal trunks and air sacs.
source: The planthopper has a simplified tracheal system without ventral longitudinal trunks and air sacs that are often found in insects with well-developed flight ability (Gunn, 1931).
evidence: The discussion section describes the simplified tracheal system with a citation.

claim: A simple tracheal system is able to satisfy the need of oxygen during flight in N. lugens.
source: Obviously, a simple tracheal system is able to satisfy the need of oxygen during flight.
evidence: The discussion section infers functional adequacy from the observation of simplified tracheal system and known flight capability.

claim: The small body size of N. lugens allows efficient oxygen diffusion.
source: This may be partly due to the small body size of N. lugens that allows efficient oxygen diffusion.
evidence: The discussion section proposes a mechanism based on physical principles and body size.
